osirisrex.name: OSIRIS-REx
osirisrex.eyebrow: NASA · New Frontiers · Asteroid sample return
osirisrex.intro: A dark, rocky asteroid held clues to the early solar system. OSIRIS-REx mapped Bennu, touched its surprisingly loose surface and sent a sealed collection of dust and pebbles back to Earth.
osirisrex.heroAlt: Illustration of the OSIRIS-REx spacecraft and its solar arrays

status.title: Sample delivered · 24 September 2023
status.body: The OSIRIS-REx sample-return phase is complete. The main spacecraft continued as OSIRIS-APEX toward Apophis; the returned Bennu material remains an active subject of laboratory research.

stats.label: Returned bulk sample
stats.note: More than twice the 60 g mission requirement

exploration.title: A journey with two endings
exploration.intro: Choose a stage to follow the sample home and discover why the spacecraft itself kept going.
exploration.description: Conceptual journey from Earth to Bennu, returning a sample capsule to Earth while the spacecraft continues to Apophis
exploration.note: Story diagram: trajectories, positions and sizes are illustrative. The Apophis leg belongs to OSIRIS-APEX and is a planned future encounter, not a completed result.

stops.name: Leaving Earth
stops.body: A 2016 launch began the journey. An Earth gravity assist in September 2017 helped align the spacecraft’s trajectory with Bennu’s orbit.
stops.factLabel: Cruise from launch to Bennu arrival
stops.question: Interplanetary navigation is about matching a moving target’s orbit, not pointing at where it appears in the sky today.

stops.name: Touching Bennu
stops.body: After mapping the boulder-covered surface, the team selected Nightingale. A sampling head briefly contacted the surface and released nitrogen to mobilise loose material.
stops.question: A spacecraft can collect a sample without settling onto the ground: make contact, capture material and back away.

stops.name: A capsule comes home
stops.body: Only the sample capsule entered Earth’s atmosphere. It descended under parachute in Utah, then the material was transferred to a dedicated curation facility.
stops.question: Keeping samples clean preserves fragile chemical clues and lets laboratories investigate questions no onboard instrument could answer alone.

stops.name: Onward to Apophis
stops.body: The spacecraft flew past Earth after releasing the capsule. Renamed OSIRIS-APEX, it is headed for a new asteroid investigation following Apophis’ 2029 Earth encounter.
stops.question: This extension will investigate a different asteroid. It is not a second sample-return mission and does not carry another return capsule.

timeline.title: A collector leaves home
timeline.body: OSIRIS-REx launches toward an encounter with the carbon-rich asteroid Bennu.

timeline.title: Meeting Bennu
timeline.body: Arrival begins close-range surveys; the first orbit insertion follows on 31 December.

timeline.title: A brief touch
timeline.body: The TAGSAM mechanism collects material at Nightingale before the spacecraft retreats from the surface.

timeline.title: Asteroid material on Earth
timeline.body: The capsule lands in Utah. The main spacecraft continues its journey under the OSIRIS-APEX mission name.

osirisrex.scienceTitle: An ancient asteroid, a modern laboratory
osirisrex.scienceIntro: The returned material connects remote observations of Bennu with measurements made using instruments on Earth.

science.title: A loosely held world
science.body: Bennu’s rocky surface was less resistant than expected during sampling. The encounter revealed why the mechanical behaviour of a rubble-pile asteroid cannot be inferred from its appearance alone.

science.title: Ingredients, not organisms
science.body: Analyses reported amino acids, nucleobases and minerals associated with ancient brines. These findings investigate prebiotic chemistry and water’s history; they do not demonstrate life on Bennu.

science.title: A collection for future questions
science.body: Curators document, protect and allocate the material for research. Preserving part of a returned sample allows future scientists to use methods and ask questions that do not yet exist.

osirisrex.instrumentIntro: Cameras, spectroscopy and laser ranging characterised Bennu before sampling. TAGSAM was the collection mechanism, not a separate remote-sensing instrument.

instruments.name: OCAMS
instruments.body: PolyCam, MapCam and SamCam imaged the asteroid, supported navigation and documented sampling.

instruments.name: OVIRS + OTES
instruments.body: Visible/infrared and thermal-emission spectroscopy investigated minerals and surface properties.

instruments.name: OLA + REXIS
instruments.body: A laser altimeter mapped shape and topography; an X-ray imaging spectrometer investigated surface elements.

instruments.name: TAGSAM
instruments.body: The articulated sampling arm and collector gathered material during brief surface contact.

instrumentDetails: The three-camera suite served different scales and tasks: long-range acquisition, global mapping, and close-up documentation of the sampling event.
Spectra reveal how materials absorb, reflect or emit light at different wavelengths. Combined with images, they help connect composition with local terrain.
The Canadian-built OLA measured laser round-trip times to construct a 3D surface map. The student-built REXIS used X-ray observations to investigate elemental composition.
A burst of nitrogen stirred regolith into the collector. The mechanism then carried the sample to the return capsule for the journey to Earth.

communication.title: A touch Earth could not control live
communication.body: Signals between Earth and Bennu took many minutes. The spacecraft carried out the sampling sequence using onboard navigation rather than waiting for a human response after each manoeuvre.
communication.note: The calculator uses an example interplanetary distance. It does not track OSIRIS-REx, its returned capsule or the current OSIRIS-APEX spacecraft.

faq.question: Did the whole spacecraft return to Earth?
faq.answer: No. It released a capsule containing the sample and diverted past Earth. The spacecraft continues as OSIRIS-APEX; the Bennu sample is studied in laboratories.

faq.question: Why collect a sample when we already have meteorites?
faq.answer: A controlled return provides a documented source and sampling context while limiting uncontrolled exposure to Earth’s environment. Researchers can compare laboratory measurements with observations of the original site.

faq.question: Will OSIRIS-APEX bring home an Apophis sample?
faq.answer: No sample return is planned for the extension. Its purpose is to investigate Apophis and how the asteroid changes around its close Earth encounter in 2029.

gaia.name: Gaia
gaia.tagline: Putting the stars in their place
gaia.eyebrow: ESA · Astrometry · A census of our Galaxy
gaia.intro: A point of light becomes a place in three dimensions. By repeatedly measuring stars’ positions, brightness and spectra, Gaia transformed the sky into a map of the Milky Way’s structure, motion and history.
gaia.heroAlt: Illustration of ESA’s Gaia spacecraft with its circular sunshield
gaia.modelNote: Schematic 3D model by OrbitLight, based on ESA references. Shapes and details are simplified; this is not an engineering model.

status.title: Spacecraft retired · 27 March 2025
status.body: Science observations ended on 15 January 2025. Gaia was then moved away from L2 into a retirement orbit around the Sun and switched off. Processing and publication of its collected data continue.

stats.label: Observed objects
stats.note: Stars and other sources over the mission

stats.label: Camera
stats.note: A focal plane shared by the science measurements

exploration.title: The sky has more than two dimensions
exploration.intro: Choose a layer to see how positions, motion and spectra turn points of light into a scientific map.
exploration.description: Illustrative star-map layers for distance, stellar motion, spectra and the Gaia catalogue
exploration.note: Conceptual all-sky illustration, not a Gaia data plot. Stars, arrows and marker locations are synthetic and represent scientific topics, not specific observed sources.

stops.name: Distances
stops.body: A nearby star appears to shift against the background as the observer travels around the Sun. Gaia used repeated measurements to separate this annual parallax from other motion.
stops.factLabel: Parsecs when parallax is in arcseconds
stops.question: A small apparent shift means a large distance. Try the parallax experiment below to see this relationship yourself.

stops.name: Stellar motion
stops.body: Proper motion describes a star’s changing direction on the sky. Radial velocity measures movement toward or away from us; together with distance they reveal motion through space.
stops.factLabel: Requires more than a position on the sky
stops.question: A star can have a small sideways drift but a large speed along our line of sight. Different measurements reveal different components.

stops.name: Light and chemistry
stops.body: Splitting starlight into wavelengths provides clues to temperature, composition and intervening dust. These properties help reconstruct where stars formed and how the Galaxy evolved.
stops.question: A red appearance can reflect a cooler star or dust along the line of sight. Interpreting the spectrum helps untangle the possibilities.

stops.name: The public archive
stops.body: The Gaia catalogue connects repeated observations with calibrated stellar properties. Published releases represent defined observing periods, not a live snapshot of every star.
stops.factLabel: A resource for research beyond the spacecraft’s lifetime
stops.question: Ending observations does not end discovery. Processing, validation and new questions continue to extract science from the stored measurements.

parallax.title: Move the viewpoint. Find the distance.
parallax.intro: Change the model star’s distance and switch between observations six months apart. More distant stars show a smaller apparent shift.
parallax.diagram: Simplified parallax geometry showing two observing positions around the Sun and a star projected against a distant background
parallax.note: Illustrative geometry: distances and angular shifts are exaggerated for visibility. The two epochs span roughly 2 AU; p is the half-amplitude of the annual parallax, not the full displacement.
parallax.explanation: This ideal example assumes an exact positive parallax. Real catalogue estimates need uncertainties and calibration; simply inverting a noisy or negative parallax can give misleading distances.

timeline.title: A surveyor leaves Earth
timeline.body: Gaia launches from French Guiana toward its observing orbit near Sun–Earth L2.

timeline.title: The first catalogue
timeline.body: Data Release 1 opens Gaia’s first star catalogue to the scientific community.

timeline.title: A richer portrait
timeline.body: Data Release 3 expands the archive with spectra, velocities, astrophysical properties and many kinds of variable sources.

timeline.title: The spacecraft retires
timeline.body: After science observations ended in January, final operations place Gaia in a retirement orbit and switch it off.

gaia.scienceIntro: Gaia observes from inside the Milky Way. Its map is assembled source by source, rather than photographed from outside the Galaxy.

science.title: Reconstructing galactic history
science.body: Stellar positions, velocities and chemistry help identify populations and past interactions. The Galaxy’s history survives in the motions of its stars.

science.title: Mapping what lies between stars
science.body: Dust dims and reddens starlight. Measurements across many sightlines reveal intervening material and help researchers distinguish it from the stars’ own properties.

science.title: A survey beyond stars
science.body: Gaia DR3 also includes positions and orbits for more than 150,000 asteroids. Its repeated sky survey links stellar astronomy with the study of our own solar system.

gaia.instrumentIntro: Two telescopes fed a shared focal plane. These cards describe the optical system and its three main science functions, rather than four independent telescopes.

instruments.name: Two viewing directions
instruments.body: Telescopes separated by a basic angle of 106.5° linked measurements across widely separated regions of the sky.

instruments.name: SM + AF
instruments.body: The sky mapper and astrometric field detected sources and measured their positions as they crossed the focal plane.

instruments.name: BP + RP
instruments.body: Blue and red photometers dispersed light to measure colour and low-resolution spectra.

instruments.name: RVS
instruments.body: The radial-velocity spectrometer measured spectral shifts for a subset of sufficiently bright sources.

instrumentDetails: Comparing both fields of view helped build a global network of stellar positions. Stable optics and repeated scans were essential to turning these angles into a coherent catalogue.
As Gaia rotated, source images drifted across CCD detectors. The timing and location of those crossings supported the astrometric solution for positions, parallaxes and proper motions.
Prisms spread light into blue and red wavelength ranges. Calibrated spectra help estimate physical properties and account for colour-dependent instrumental effects.
The Doppler shift of spectral features constrains velocity along the line of sight. Not every catalogue source has an RVS measurement, so the available information differs between stars.

communication.eyebrow: An archive built from repeated scans
communication.title: From the focal plane to a catalogue
communication.body: During operations, Gaia sent its observations through ESA’s ground network. Processing combined many crossings of each source with spacecraft calibration to derive reliable positions and properties.
communication.note: The signal calculator uses the approximate historical Earth–L2 distance as an example. Gaia is now switched off in a heliocentric retirement orbit; this is not its current range.

faq.question: Is Gaia still observing near L2?
faq.answer: No. Science observations ended on 15 January 2025. The spacecraft left the L2 region and was switched off on 27 March 2025 in a retirement orbit around the Sun.

faq.question: Is Gaia’s map a photograph of our Galaxy from outside?
faq.answer: No. Gaia observed from within the Milky Way. All-sky maps combine measured sources; external views of the Galaxy are reconstructions or artist impressions and should be labelled accordingly.

faq.question: Does every source have a full distance and 3D velocity?
faq.answer: No. Available measurements and their precision vary by source and data release. Reliable distance and velocity studies must account for uncertainties, selection effects and which parameters were actually published.
